This vote was on accepting the Senate's changes, which sends the bill to the President. A Yea accepts the Senate version; a Nay rejects it.

votes.bill_title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
votes.plain_language: This bill provides appropriations to several federal departments and agencies for the remainder of FY2026 and provides continuing FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security through February 13, 2026. A Yea supports passing it in the House; a Nay opposes it.

votes.question: On Agreeing to the Amendment (H R 7148)
votes.bill_title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
votes.plain_language: This amendment to H.R. 7148 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) is summarized by the Congressional Research Service as: “Amendment sought to prohibit the use of funds for certain community funding projects.” A Yea supports adding it to the bill; a Nay opposes it.

votes.question: On Agreeing to the Amendment (H R 7148)
votes.bill_title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
votes.plain_language: This amendment to H.R. 7148 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026) is summarized by the Congressional Research Service as: “Amendment sought to prohibit the use of funds to implement section 24220 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, including any requirements enabling or supporting vehicle "kill switch" technology, and to prohibit federal spending for the execution or enforcement of such authorities.” A Yea supports adding it to the bill; a Nay opposes it.

votes.question: On Passage — Making further consolidated appropriations for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes (H R 7147)
votes.bill_title: Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026.
votes.plain_language: This bill provides continuing FY2026 appropriations to the Department of Homeland Security through May 22, 2026. A Yea supports passing it in the House; a Nay opposes it.

votes.plain_language: This bill provides FY2026 appropriations to several federal departments and agencies for activities and programs related to financial services, general government, national security, the administration of foreign affairs, and foreign assistance. A Yea supports passing it in the House; a Nay opposes it.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended — AGOA Extension Act (H R 6500)

votes.plain_language: This bill provides continuing FY2027 appropriations for federal agencies and extends various expiring programs and authorities. This vote was under suspension of the rules, so a two-thirds vote was required. A Yea supports passing it as amended; a Nay opposes it.

posts.text: Our troops risk their lives to defend our nation. Toxic burn pit exposure should never leave them fighting another battle long after they return home.  That is why I helped introduce the bipartisan WIPE OUT Burn Pits Act to identify and track dangerous burn pits near U.S. forces,

Children battling rare diseases cannot afford to wait. A rare diagnosis should never mean a child is left behind in the search for lifesaving treatments.  My bipartisan Priority for Pediatric Cures Actwould permanently authorize the FDA’s Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Voucher Program, giving researchers and innovators the long-term certainty needed to invest in treatments for children with few or no options.  Developing a treatment can take years, but investment decisions are being made today. Families deserve hope, and promising research deserves the opportunity to move forward.  I urge my colleagues to expedite passage of this critical legislation. Every child deserves a chance at a healthier future. Let’s get this done!

It was a pleasure to meet with Cory Price, the new Director of James A. Haley Veterans’ Hospital, and his leadership team to discuss concerns local Veterans have shared with me. Their experiences guide my work to improve access to timely, high-quality care and ensure their concerns receive the attention they deserve.  I was encouraged by updates on construction at the new Lecanto and Brooksville clinics, as well as the new Community Living Center in Lutz. These projects represent important investments in care for Veterans throughout our region.  I also appreciated Director Price’s commitment to improving the VA’s regional phone system, which has been a persistent source of frustration for many Veterans, and his willingness to address concerns about declining referrals to the Veteran Directed Care program.  I look forward to building a strong working relationship with Director Price and his team, maintaining open communication, and working together to address the challenges facing Veterans and their families. Those who served our nation deserve a VA that listens, responds, and delivers.

On October 28, we commemorate Oxi Day and honor the courage of the Greek people, who stood against fascism in 1940 with a resounding “OXI”—“NO!” Their refusal to surrender their freedom remains an enduring example of bravery, unity, and sacrifice. Their example reminds us that freedom requires courage and that standing up to tyranny matters, even against overwhelming odds.  May we honor their legacy by defending liberty and passing their remarkable story on to future generations.

Veterans battling a devastating disease shouldn’t also have to battle bureaucracy for the benefits they’ve earned.  I’m proud to lead a bipartisan, bicameral letter, joined by 53 lawmakers, urging the VA to recognize Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM) as a presumptive service-connected condition. This would help Veterans living with this rare, progressive, incurable muscle disease access disability benefits without individually proving their illness is linked to military service.  Our Veterans deserve answers, fair treatment, and timely support. I’ll keep fighting for them.

I enjoyed stopping by “Made in the USA: Tampa Bay’s Role in Saving American Shipping” for an important discussion with the Shipbuilders Council of America and the Maritime Alliance about strengthening our nation’s shipbuilding industry.  We discussed the SHIPS for America Act, the importance of the Jones Act, and the national security implications of relying on foreign shipbuilding and maritime capabilities. A strong American maritime industry is essential to our economic security, resilient supply chains, and national defense - and Tampa Bay has an important role to play.  The conversation also highlighted the need to invest in the skilled workforce that makes this industry possible. Expanding training opportunities and building pathways into maritime careers will help ensure we have the welders, engineers, shipbuilders, and other skilled professionals needed to keep America competitive. I remain committed to supporting American workers and strengthening our nation’s maritime capabilities.

funding.detail: Federal cards show the principal campaign committee and OpenFEC totals for one two-year cycle, plus itemized Schedule A contributors. House uses 2026. Senate uses the cycle of the next election (2026, 2028, or 2030). This is not career fundraising and does not include Schedule E outside spending. Governors do not get a federal contribution list.
